analysis.one_liner: Caps prices of drugs developed with federal research dollars to 'reasonable pricing' agreements.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote: it sat in the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health until the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: When federal agencies or nonprofits develop a drug with taxpayer-funded research, the bill would block them from handing over the patent until the patent holder signs a 'reasonable pricing' agreement with the Department of Health and Human Services. It also requires that Uncle Sam be charged no more than the lowest price charged in comparable wealthy countries, and bans terms that favor foreign buyers over Americans. Taxpayers currently help fund medical research, then often pay high drug prices for the medicines that result.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers and patients. Anyone who needs a drug developed with public research dollars would benefit from a formal promise that prices stay 'reasonable', and the federal government would be guaranteed the lowest price charged in comparable OECD countries. The public would also get notice and a chance to comment before any waiver from these requirements.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and patients needing publicly funded drugs

how_it_helps.text: Bars any federal agency or nonprofit from conveying a patent on a drug, biologic, or other health technology developed through federally funded research until the patent recipient agrees to a reasonable pricing agreement with the Secretary of Health and Human Services [S3].

Requires that the federal government be charged no more than the lowest price charged to the wealthiest OECD countries with per capita income at least half that of the United States, ending the situation where Americans pay more than foreign buyers for the same drug [S3].
Prohibits pricing terms that give foreign purchasers better access or conditions than Americans get, including supply limits that disadvantage domestic buyers [S3].
Requires public notice and a comment period before the Secretary can waive the pricing requirement, with a written finding that the waiver serves the public interest [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical and biotech companies that take patents on taxpayer-funded drug discoveries would no longer be free to set whatever price they choose on those products, and could earn less on them. They would also argue that price caps on such drugs reduce the return that funds their next round of research.

drawbacks.text: Reasonable pricing agreements can be slow and contentious to negotiate, and the bill gives no timeline, so a drug's patent transfer could be delayed while pricing is argued over [S3].
The requirement applies only to drugs developed with federally funded research, so it would leave most brand-name drug prices untouched and would not fix the broader pricing problem on its own [S2].

Critics of such agreements, including industry groups, argue that lower returns on specific discoveries could reduce the incentive to license and commercialize taxpayer-funded discoveries in the first place; the bill text does not address this objection.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core bargain is straightforward: the public already pays for the research, so the public gets a promise the resulting medicine is priced reasonably rather than whatever the market will bear. The limits are real but narrow — it touches only the slice of drug development that flows from federally funded research, and a waiver process with public notice (rather than an outright ban on high pricing) gives the Secretary room to approve exceptions. On net, a modest, targeted check on drug pricing with limited downside for ordinary people.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, sent to its Health Subcommittee, and never received a markup or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter DeFazio introduced the bill on July 28, 2017, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S1].
It was referred to the Subcommittee on Health on August 4, 2017, and no further action was recorded for the remainder of the 115th Congress [S5].
The bill drew 7 cosponsors, all Democrats [S4].
The Congress ended January 3, 2019, without the bill ever advancing out of committee [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical and biotech patent holders keep the ability to price taxpayer-funded discoveries without a pricing commitment; no other group gained anything because nothing changed in law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug patent holders, who never faced the pricing terms

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out of committee or scheduled a markup during the 115th Congress

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Controls the House floor calendar in the 115th Congress
against.what_they_did: Bills that clear committee in this Congress generally need leadership to schedule floor time, which never happened for this bill

sides.party_line_note: All seven cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republican support recorded, and the bill died in a House controlled by Republicans without any vote [S4][S5].

industries.note: Companies receiving patents on federally funded drug discoveries would have had to agree to 'reasonable' prices and match the lowest comparable OECD price for federal purchases. The bill died in committee, so the status quo — no pricing conditions on taxpayer-funded patents — continued.

The bill would have conditioned their ability to convey patents on signing pricing agreements, adding a requirement and potentially reducing licensing revenue, while reflecting the argument that publicly funded discoveries should be priced for public benefit.
